newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Markets react to "forgettable" Australian budget.
newsitem.headline: Markets react to "forgettable" Australian budget.

text.p: The Australian dollar fell back from earlier gains on Tuesday as markets reacted to what was described as a "forgettable" mid-term budget delivered by Treasurer Peter Costello.
Traders had hoped for a tight budget and the Australian dollar was bid higher through the day amid speculation of heavy spending cuts and large surpluses.
Costello later disappointed markets by delivering a modest second budget for the conservative Australian government.
By 8.45 p.m. (1045 GMT) the dollar had lost all the day's gains, falling to US$0.7772/77 from US$0.7826/31 just before the budget details hit dealing screens an hour earlier.
"The market was hoping for a memorable event, but all it got was a forgettable budget," said Steve Shuster, head of foreign exchange at Citibank Australia.
Debt dealers also felt let down and the June 10-year bond futures contract eased to 92.290 from 92.360 just prior to Treasurer Peter Costello handing down the budget.
The share market was long closed when Costello began to deliver his budget speech in parliament but share futures barely budged in a special after-hours session.
The equities market saw little in the budget either way and the June Share Price Index (SPI) contract was idling at 2,543, four points weaker than its official close.
"The main complaint will be the government has done the bare minimum in terms of spending cuts," said David Bassanese, an economist at Bankers Trust Australia.
Median expectations had been the government would chop between A$1.5-2.0 billion from the underlying deficit for 1997/98, leaving a shortfall of around A$2.0 billion.
Costello's budget delivered net savings of A$352 million, leaving the deficit at A$3.9 billion.
"Markets always want a pleasant surprise on budgets and this time they didn't get one," said Bassanese. "You'd have to say there's not enough in this budget to earn a credit upgrade."

Ratings agency Standard and Poor's put Australia on positive creditwatch following last year's eye-wateringly tight budget, and the market had thought a decent savings effort this time might earn an improvement its credit rating.

Commodity prices had also picked up recently with the influential Commodity Research Bureau index on Monday hitting a high for the year. Commodities make up over 60 percent of Australia's exports and the currency tends to track prices.
